title: ticfac Phase 2: the Herdr executor
description:
SPEC §12 Phase 2 (ticks tick jrj). The Herdr executor behind the SAME four
operations Phase 1 defined, plus the two local ones — so the reconciler learns
nothing about panes, workspaces or protocols.

Scope, from jrj:
- A Herdr executor implementing Start / Inspect / CollectDetail / Cancel /
  Dispose, with its private addressing inside JobHandle.handle (the one open
  object in the contract).
- Move execution-oriented Herdr process and fleet helpers out of ticks'
  internal/herd/**; leave tracker-domain configuration and the question relay
  in ticks.
- Support a RANGE of Herdr protocol versions: hard floor, warn version, no
  upper bound.
- Move internal/factory/** and the Factory commands to the ticfac CLI, with no
  hidden tk dispatch shims.
- Replace every ticks internal Go import with `tk --json`, Git, or a pinned
  schema.

Four constraints carried from the Phase 1 retro, drawn from what actually broke
in the existing herd orchestrator during the Phase 1 run:

1. The verdict lives in DURABLE EVIDENCE, never in the substrate. Phase 1's
   executor decides from a report on disk, commits on a branch, and an exit
   code, and refuses to read process chatter as liveness. The Herdr executor
   inherits that rule. Then a Herdr upgrade can cost a dispatch but can never
   corrupt a result. The existing spawn gate — which types into a composer and
   reads the pane back for an echo — violates it, and misreported an account
   capacity failure as a broken composer during the Phase 1 run.
2. Protocol trouble is OPERATIONAL, never a verdict. A version mismatch or a
   missing capability must not reject a tick or tear an attempt down.
3. Capability is checked at Start and refused BY NAME. Phase 1 already checks
   the host can honour the executor a profile names; extend that to the
   protocol range and the operations needed, naming the Herdr version and the
   missing operation in the refusal.
4. The substrate goes in PROVENANCE. Executor, model and profile digest are
   already recorded; add the Herdr protocol and server version, so a run that
   spans an upgrade can be diagnosed rather than guessed at.

The hazard to design for first is RESUME ACROSS AN UPGRADE: a job started under
one protocol that the next leg cannot address. Hold it for a person. Never
redispatch — the old worker may still be alive and spending.

Open design question this epic must settle: ticfac reads `[roles.*]` from the
target repository's `.tick/runners.toml` directly, which is a second coupling to
ticks alongside the `tk --json` + pinned-bundle rule. Deliberate in Phase 1 and
carefully mitigated (the roles reader is a separate reader that can run nothing),
but a second substrate multiplies it.

Plan the child ticks at the start of this epic, not now.
notes:
2026-09-10 10:58 - decision: Tier is chosen per dispatch by the orchestrator, which is how a run ends up on a more advanced tier than the work justified. Make it deterministic — but does that need a tier field in ticks? → No new tracker field. Derive the tier in ticfac from tracker facts that already exist (priority, type, process role, labels, graph position), with a declared ticfac-side policy, a default-then-escalate-on-failure ladder, and an opaque LABEL as the override. Tick 5eq. — Separates the inputs from the policy. The facts a tick already carries are legitimately the tracker's own and describe the work; the mapping from those facts to a runner and a model is orchestration and belongs in ticfac, which is the direction Phase 2 exists to push. A label keeps the storage generic — ticks stores an opaque string and has no idea what it means — so the semantics stay wholly in ticfac, unlike a real field which would make the tracker complicit. The escalation ladder is what actually fixes the complaint: nothing can START high, because a first attempt takes the default tier and only a failed attempt escalates. Cost accepted and written into the tick: a label is weakly typed, ticks cannot validate it, so an unrecognised tier label must be refused loudly rather than silently defaulting.
2026-09-10 11:22 - decision: Pi is reachable as a herdr kind but carries no verified full-auto template, so a role routed to it starts without one and can stall on a permission prompt. Where does verifying it belong? → In Phase 2 as tick sur, not in the ticks tracker. The capability matrix is execution config and becomes ticfac's under this epic; sur is blocked behind the config split so the pi row lands beside the roles and tiers tables. — Filing it against ticks would put new execution config into the repository this epic exists to take it out of, and the row would then have to be moved again by the config split. The live round-trip can be run against the current ticks code at any time; what must LAND is the verified template, and that belongs where the matrix will live. Verified 2026-09-10 by exercising Compile directly: a provider-qualified cloudflare id compiles to --model cloudflare-workers-ai/@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3:high and every compile warns that pi has no verified full-auto template — a warning, not a refusal, so a run starts and may hang. Local pi 0.85.1 reports the cloudflare-workers-ai provider ready with an api_key and lists 18 of its models, so the provider side is genuinely set up and only the herdr-side template is missing.
2026-09-10 11:24 - decision: How does a tier specify WHICH pi model it uses, robustly? pi is cross-provider, so a tier naming a model is only meaningful if that model is what actually runs. → No new syntax — a tier overlay already sets kind, model and effort together, as the balanced tier does for codex. Robustness comes from three checks folded into tick sur: answer empirically whether pi silently substitutes an unknown id, validate the id against pi's own catalog rather than a slash check, and refuse an effort level on a model whose catalog says it has no thinking dimension. — The configuration mechanism is not the weak part; the guarantees behind it are. opencode was caught running a whole turn on its default after being given an unknown model id, passing the first-round-trip gate cleanly, with only the pane footer betraying it — so 'the tier named a model' proves nothing until we know pi's behaviour on a bad id. Verified today that pi ships a real oracle for this (pi --list-models prints provider, model and a per-model thinking column, and reports 'No models matching' for an unknown one) while pi auth check --model reports ready for a nonsense id and is therefore NOT a model oracle. The existing validator only asks whether a slash appears anywhere, so every typo passes. And because pi takes effort as a suffix on the model id rather than a flag, an effort level on a non-thinking model is the same class of error opencode's row already refuses rather than silently drops.
2026-09-10 11:28 - decision: Does the wall-clock bound come for free from Phase 1 for a herdr worker, or does the herdr executor have to enforce it? → The executor must enforce it. The deadline is inherited, the kill is not — added to tick d9m, and a bound that cannot be enforced through the available herdr protocol is a refusal at dispatch. — Phase 1 splits noticing a deadline from enforcing one across exactly the seam Phase 2 implements. The settlement deadline is reconciler-side (dispatch.go:971, issued + WallSeconds + wipe threshold) and does carry over, so a quiet herdr worker is declared settled on schedule. But the kill lives in the executor, because the local one owns the process it started (subprocess/inspect.go:131, collect.go:177). A herdr worker's process belongs to herdr, so nothing inherited stops it: the reconciler would declare the attempt settled and move on while the agent keeps running and keeps spending, with the run's own records saying it is over. That is worse than no bound, because the operator believes in it. Refusing at dispatch when the bound cannot be enforced is the same fail-closed discipline the rest of the epic uses.
2026-09-10 11:38 - decision: sur was blocked behind the config split, but the live round trip that makes pi usable as a worker needs nothing from it. That left pi unavailable for the whole first half of the epic for no reason. Split it? → Split into gjk (verify pi live, unblocked, attended, lands no config) and sur (land the verified row and its validators, still behind wgi). gjk joins wave 1. — The work that makes pi usable cannot be given to pi, so it has to be attended and it has to be early — a chicken-and-egg the original single tick made worse by putting it in wave 3. Only the LANDING of the row depends on the config split; the round trip, the substitution probe and the effort-suffix probe depend on nothing. Splitting makes pi available from wave 2 instead of wave 4, and it also separates evidence from config, which is the same discipline the rest of the epic uses: gjk produces findings with the commands and output that produced them, and sur writes a row it can point at rather than one somebody reasoned out.
2026-09-10 11:39 - decision: Which tier should Phase 2 implementation ticks run at, given the operator trusts GLM 5.3 / 5.3-flash on cloudflare for any tick? → Operator's standing preference: GLM 5.3 or 5.3-flash via pi for implementation ticks once pi is verified (gjk), with a frontier-tier review at epic completion. Until gjk lands, wave 1 runs at the DEFAULT tier and escalates only on failure. — The operator states GLM 5.3 and 5.3-flash are close to state of the art and is willing to trust any tick to them provided the epic gets a frontier-level review at completion — which the epic already has as tick zus. Recording it here makes it the input to tick 5eq's declared policy rather than a per-dispatch judgement call, which is the whole point of 5eq. It cannot apply yet: pi carries no verified full-auto template, so a role routed to it starts without one and can stall, which is exactly what gjk determines. Applying default-then-escalate to wave 1 now is the same ladder 5eq will encode, exercised by hand.
2026-09-10 12:49 - decision: How should the rest of Phase 2 be routed? → Operator routing, now encoded in .tick/runners.toml: GLM 5.3 on cloudflare via pi is the DEFAULT implement role for complex work; GLM 5.3-flash is the economy tier for simple mechanical work; opus is the strong tier, reserved for escalation after a failed attempt; and review and closeout have their own opus tables. — Records the operator's instruction as configuration rather than as a per-dispatch judgement call, which is the point of tick 5eq — the file is now the policy, and an orchestrator evaluates it instead of choosing. Verified by resolving every route through the real spawn path: implement gives glm-5.3:high with --approve, economy gives glm-5.3-flash:medium, strong gives opus with bypassPermissions, and review and closeout both give opus. Honest note on classification: almost everything remaining in Phase 2 is complex — the protocol hardening, the executor, the config split, the tier policy and the retirement all turn on judgement. The economy tier is there for mechanical sub-ticks such as those the v3i split will produce, not for the current frontier.
2026-09-10 12:49 - runners.toml defect found while encoding the routing: tier overlays INHERIT args from the base role, so a tier that changes kind inherits flags the new kind cannot parse — the opus 'strong' tier was resolving to 'claude ... --approve', a pi flag. Fixed by clearing args = [] on every tier that changes kind. Worth carrying into tick wgi when the roles tables move to ticfac: inheriting args across a kind change should probably be a refusal rather than something an operator has to remember.
2026-09-10 12:51 - decision: Correction to the Phase 2 routing: is opus an escalation tier for implementation? → No. Implementation runs entirely on GLM through pi — 5.3 for complex work (the default and the strong tier) and 5.3-flash for simple work. opus is the claude harness only, reserved for review and closeout, and is not available in the pi harness at all. — My first encoding made opus the strong tier as an escalation target for failed attempts, which the operator corrected: opus is for the epic review, not for implementation. That also removes an assumption the escalation ladder in tick 5eq was resting on — there is no cross-harness escalation to reach for, so the ladder for this epic is within GLM (flash to 5.3, and effort within a model), and a tick that fails at 5.3 is a signal for a person rather than for a bigger model. 5eq should encode that rather than a generic 'escalate one step'. Verified after the change by resolving every route through the real spawn path: implement, economy and strong all give pi with a GLM model; review and closeout give claude with opus.
2026-09-10 13:27 - Operational finding, wave 2 on cloudflare Workers AI: one of four concurrent GLM-5.3 workers (jv7) hit HTTP 429 with no body, retried 3 times immediately, and gave up — the run stalled until nudged. The other three never saw a 429. Cloudflare publishes a per-account requests-per-minute cap for Workers AI (developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/platform/limits), and an agent in a tool loop makes many requests per minute, so four concurrent workers plausibly exceed it in bursts while any one of them alone would not. Two consequences: (1) wave width 4 is too wide for this provider — the width is a herdr/host concern today but is really a PROVIDER concern, and belongs in the routing policy tick 5eq alongside the tier; (2) pi retried 3 times with no backoff, which turns a transient burst limit into a dead worker. Retry-with-backoff on 429 is the difference between a pause and a stall, and it is the same fail-open-to-a-stall shape the epic is already chasing.
acceptance_criteria: The operator runs a real ticks epic for actual work through ticfac run-epic on Herdr, instead of the tk herd skill ritual, and it completes. The reconciler contains no Herdr-specific code: the executor interface is unchanged and Herdr addressing lives inside JobHandle.handle. A Herdr protocol version outside the supported range, or a missing capability, refuses at Start naming the Herdr version and the missing operation, and does NOT reject the tick or tear the attempt down. Every record a Herdr dispatch produces carries the Herdr protocol and server version in its provenance. An attempt started under one protocol that a later leg cannot address is held for a person and never redispatched. No ticks internal Go package is imported: every crossing is tk --json, Git, or a pinned schema. go test -short -timeout 45m ./... green (make test-short).
